speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN CONSTRUCTION OF PACIFIC COAXIAL CABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform members of the house that the government has approved, subject to further financial arrangements being satisfactorily negotiated, the participation by Canada in the construction of a multipurpose coaxial cable in the Pacific ocean between Vancouver, British Columbia, and New Zealand and Australia. Completion date will be some time in 1964, and the cable will form the second leg of the round the world commonwealth cable system. This trans-Pacific section will cost around $75 million, of which Canada's share will be approximately $25 million. Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, the crown company under the Department

of Transport, will, on behalf of Canada, own the portion of the trans-Pacific cable from Vancouver to a point approximately 2,700 miles distant from Canada. The section beyond that point to Sydney, Australia, will be owned jointly by Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom.

It will be recalled that on June 19 last I informed the house that the Japanese government had suspended the issuing of new licences for the export to Canada of a broad range of textile products. This suspension followed an extraordinary increase in Japanese exports to Canada of these products heavily concentrated in a narrow range of items. Following that announcement, discussions took place between the Canadian and Japanese authorities concerning the basis upon which the trade in these items would be resumed. On August 16 I announced the conclusion of those discussions and described in detail the quotas which would be applied for the rest of 1959. I also indicated that the Japanese authorities had undertaken to consult the Canadian government before making their decisions on the 1960 quotas. In addition to certain textile products, Japan also maintains export restraints on shipments to Canada of plywood and stainless steel flatware. The current discussions relate to the products now under control together with several others.
Consultations between Japan and Canada on the quotas for 1960 have been in progress for a number of weeks. It had been our hope that these discussions would be completed before the end of December in order that the industries in both countries would be able to plan their lines of production for 1960. A great deal of detailed and technical work is, however, involved and it has not been possible to complete the consultations as quickly as we had hoped. The government regards these consultations as urgent and important and it is intended that they should be concluded as quickly as possible. As the Prime Minister indicated to the house on January 22, my colleagues and I had an opportunity to discuss these problems with the Japanese Prime Minister and the Japanese foreign minister during their visit to Ottawa. They readily recognized the need to complete these consultations quickly.
Japanese exports to Canada are concentrated very heavily in the textile field and several other manufactured products such as plywood and stainless steel flatware. In 1959, for example, approximately 40 per cent of Japan's exports to Canada were textiles. Moreover, within the general category of textiles the impact is concentrated on a rather limited number of products, particularly garments. This concentration adds greatly to the difficulties Canadian producers of these products would in any case experience as a result of the rapid expansion of Japanese exports.

From the time we entered into a trade agreement, the Japanese have recognized that the growth of their exports to Canada must proceed on an orderly basis and that they must avoid disruption of Canadian markets which would result from excessive concentration and too rapid and extensive penetration. This is the reason why in their own interest they have introduced restraints on exports of particularly sensitive products to Canada.
When we speak of orderly growth, both countries have agreed that they have in mind for individual products which are competitive with Canadian production increases of about 5 to 10 per cent in a good year, that is a year in which the Canadian economy is buoyant and demand for the products in question is rising. This does not mean that imports should increase by this amount in products where our market has already been flooded; nor does it mean that larger increases can never be accepted for products where the Canadian industry is not experiencing difficulties in meeting competition. In 1959, however, imports into Canada from Japan increased by almost 50 per cent over 1958. Within this over-all increase, textile imports taken together almost doubled. Imports of some items-indeed of some quite sensitive items-rose by 100 per cent or even 150 per cent, from a base that was already large. These increases are far beyond any reasonable definition of orderly growth. I emphasize this in order to make it clear why these present consultations are so necessary if we are to work out with the Japanese government export levels which will be consistent with our agreed objective of orderly growth. It is evident that there has been some misunderstanding in some quarters in Canada as to what we are seeking in these discussions.
As hon. members know, there has been a steady expansion of trade in both directions since our trade agreement came into force. Japanese sales in Canada have increased from $14 million in 1953 to approximately $105 million in 1959. Canadian exports to Japan have increased in the same period from $119 million to approximately $135 million.
Since 1955 sales of Canadian wheat and flour to Japan have gone up from $54 million to over $70 million and there are good prospects that sales of grain as well as other Canadian exports will continue to grow. The current discussions with Japan for the purpose of ensuring that Japanese exports to Canada proceed on an orderly basis will not prejudice the expansion of our sales to Japan including wheat. On the contrary, it is only by avoiding disruption of Canadian markets and damage to sensitive Canadian industries that we can look to a mutually advantageous expansion of trade with Japan on a basis

which can be sustained over the years. The Japanese government is fully aware of this position.

Mr. Speaker, reports of this nature are of a confidential quality. They are made in pursuance of the provisions of the Civil Service Act by the commission to the government through the Minister of Finance. They are confidential documents, are privileged, and have always been so treated. Their contents have never been made public except when the government has acted on recommendations; then they have been made public only when the government in announcement of such action on its part has indicated that it has been taken in accordance with the recommendations of the commission.
I have had a careful survey made of all the records. I am informed that never has any such report been made public or tabled in the house.

maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION REPORT ON PAY INCREASES, 1959
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point [DOT]of order arising out of the answer given by the minister. As I understand the procedure, a motion for the production of papers is not

debatable. It could be argued that the minister went beyond that rule in his statement of the reasons for not tabling the document, but in any event that is not the point I wish to raise. The point is that it undoubtedly is the right of a minister of the crown to refuse to produce a document on the grounds that it is not in the public interest to do so, and I presume this is what the minister was seeking to give as his reason for not tabling the document asked for in the notice of motion.
The point I wish to raise is that the discretion of a minister of the crown to refuse to table a document is applicable to those documents that come to the ministry or to a minister in the field or area of jurisdiction for which he has responsibility; that is, if it were a departmental document coming to the minister, admittedly that would be a perfectly valid answer to the notice of motion, but the situation here is a little different.
This is the point I wish to make. The report asked for is a report of the civil service commission, and the first legislation having to do with the civil service commission was set up a little more than half a century ago for the express purpose of taking away from the administration of the day the responsibility in certain civil service matters enumerated in the legislation and giving it to an independent body answerable to parliament. The civil service commission is answerable to parliament; it is not answerable to the government of the day.
I can reinforce my argument in that regard 

I do not wish to extend it unduly-by recalling to Your Honour's attention the Civil Service Act amendment which came before the House of Commons in 1918. There was a resolution preceding the amending bill; and that amending bill, I might say, was a bill bringing what was called the outside service under the jurisdiction of the civil service commission. It really meant the bringing of the civil service under the jurisdiction of the commission. I will not read the first part of the resolution. It states that it is expedient to consolidate and revise the Civil Service Act, and so on, and to provide for the salary of the chairman, and so on. This is the part to which I wish to draw Your Honour's attention:
And to make appointments to the public service upon competitive examination and otherwise eliminate political patronage in the control and management of the said service.
This is the motion which was presented to the house by Hon. A. K. M'acLean, later Mr. Justice MacLean. It will be seen that the express purpose was to make this body independent and take the control in these matters away from the government and give it to this body.

There is just one more citation I wish to give to Your Honour, if I may, to show how far they have gone in making this body independent of government control. It is provided' that the commission can only be removed from office at any time during its term of office by the Governor General on an address of the Senate and the House of Commons. This is the same method used for the judiciary and, I believe, for the Auditor General of Canada. In other words the whole scheme of the act is to take away from the ministry any right to interfere in the matters over which the commission has jurisdiction by this act, and one of these matters is a recommendation as to the pay of civil servants.
The report therefore, following the argument I have been seeking to make, belongs to parliament; it does not belong to the government. It is not a report to the government of the day; it is a report that belongs to and is the property of parliament. The minister's function, in so far as a report of this nature is concerned, is merely that of a vehicle for parliament. Since the civil service commission obviously cannot come itself to present and table the report, the minister has to do it.
There are other areas where the Minister of Finance and the government have jurisdiction under the act, but this is not one of them. That is the force of my argument.

Speaking just
briefly, I may say that the hon. gentleman, I think, is quite astray of the mark in what he has been saying about the act. It is true that the act in certain respects confers functions and authority upon the civil service commission to be discharged on their own behalf and without reference to government or to parliament; but in the matter of salaries of the civil service they are in a different situation entirely. There the act, Mr. Speaker, provides that the civil service commission may make recommendations to government. It is under a different section of the act, section 11, and the observations of the hon. gentleman are completely irrelevant to the matter here involved. It is perfectly clear, Mr. Speaker, that these reports to the government, involving as they do financial matters, have always been treated as privileged documents. They have never been tabled in the house or made public. This has been the practice of all governments that have been in office in this country since the act was first enacted in 1918.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would care to comment on the statement made by the President of the United States at his press conference this morning, just drawn to my attention, that he would like to see the United States share more of its military and atomic secrets with Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not read the statement. All I have before me is a press

bulletin story by the Canadian Press staff writer in Washington, in which the following is reported:
His statement at a press conference came amid reports that the U. S. administration may propose changes in the American law allowing such allies as Canada, Britain and France a greater degree of custody and control of TJ. S. atomic weapons stockpiled in these countries.
While not desiring to make any intensive examination of the purport of these remarks, may I say that any action in that connection would ensure the implementation of the words I used when speaking in the house on January 18, when I said, as reported at page 73 of Hansard:

speechtext:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
In the 1958 session provision was made to increase during the period of three years from January 31, 1958 the maximum contributions that may be made from the railway grade crossing fund. The provision was enacted in chapter 40 of the statutes of 1958. Prior to the passing of that act the maximum contribution from the fund toward work in respect of a level crossing, such as installation of warning devices or construction of a grade separation to eliminate the level crossing, was 60 per cent of the cost of the work, or $300,000, whichever was the lesser, and in the case of reconstruction of a grade separation already in existence it was 30 per cent, or $150,000, whichever was the lesser. The 1958 statute increased these maxima to 80 per cent and $500,000 in the case of level crossings and 50 per cent and $250,000 in the

case of reconstruction of existing grade separations, for work ordered or authorized in the three years commencing January 31, 1958. It also made provision for corresponding percentages for relocation of public utility plant is part of such work and for contributions up to 80 per cent of the cost of placing reflective markings on the sides of railway cars during that period.
Unless that three-year period is extended it will expire next January, so it is appropriate to pass legislation at this session to extend it. The purpose of the proposed legislation is to extend the period for a further three years.
In 1958 an extra $10 million was put in the fund. This was in addition to the statutory appropriation of $5 million. Another extra $10 million was voted in 1959.
This combination of increasing the fund and the maximum of the grants has encouraged and assisted projects to eliminate and reduce dangers at crossings, as I felt sure it would. I will mention just a few facts and comparisons that will indicate the increased assistance provided from the fund in the last two years and the increase in the work for the protection of the public at crossings in those years.
Of the $30 million put in the fund in the past two years, over $28 million was committed up to the end of January of this year toward projects authorized in those years, with two months of the fiscal year still left.
Another significant fact that the total amount paid out of the fund from 1909 to the end of 1957 was $19,814,110, whereas since the start of 1958 over $28 million was committed, as I said, toward projects authorized in the last two years.
Another comparison: in the ten years prior to 1958 the average number of protective devices installed per year at level crossings was about 88, compared with 253 in 1958 and 352 in 1959. The number of new grade separations and reconstructions of inadequate subways and overhead bridges, authorized in the past two years with grants from the fund, has also shown a marked increase, for the number of such projects in the last two years was 99, practically as many as the total of 102 authorized in the previous eight years.
I could go on with more details, but I do not think it is necessary, for I am confident that the bill to continue the increased maxima for another three years will be welcomed by everyone.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope I will be in order if I say how happy I am to see

you back in your usual place, and I think I speak on behalf of all hon. members of the house.
I should like to say that we on this side of the house welcome the announcement which has been made by the Minister of Transport. While he was speaking, although I may be accused of having a suspicious mind, I could not help but wonder why first priority should be given to this particular resolution, important as it is, because, as the hon. minister said, this resolution really extends the provisions of the 1958 amendment for a period of three years beyond January 31, 1961. Surely there are on the order paper a considerable number of resolutions and legislation which would have effect sooner than that. The only explanation I can find, of course, is that this is another indication of the unfathomable logic which the government has used in introducing legislation in the house, particularly this year.
But this is not to say that I do not consider the legislation important. It is important legislation and good legislation. I do not believe there is any hon. member in any corner of the house who would object seriously to what is provided in this resolution. As a matter of fact, I believe there is not one member of parliament who has not had direct knowledge of unfortunate accidents at railway crossings.
It might be interesting, in order to point out the importance of the problem, to state how many accidents there were over a period of, let us say, ten years. In the report of the board of transport commissioners of December, 1958 there is a table giving the number of highway crossing accidents and motor vehicle registrations. In 1949 there were 441 accidents; 138 people were killed and 589 were injured. In 1958 there were 518 accidents; 188 people were killed and some 660 were injured. Although the figures do not show this, there is a definite improvement in the decline of accidents and mortalities, because in 1949 there were 2,290,000-odd vehicles registered, whereas in 1957, the last date for which figures are given, there were
4,459,000.	Even though there is a definite decrease in the number of accidents on railway crossings, I think all hon. members will agree it is still a problem which we should try to solve as best we can.
I think it would be of interest to note that the basis for the legislation we are discussing this afternoon is a report of the board of transport commissioners which followed a serious investigation from coast to coast of the difficulties, both financial and technical, that the municipalities and provinces were encountering at railway crossings. After having
Railway Act
travelled throughout the country obtaining as much information as possible, the board of transport commissioners made seven or eight recommendations which were embodied into an amendment to the Railway Act in 1955. At this time they boosted the grade crossing fund from $1 million to $5 million, and they boosted the percentage from 40 to 60 per cent of the cost to be paid out of this fund for the work on level crossings. They also raised to 30 per cent the reconstruction of grade separations, et cetera.
Of course, these 1955 amendments, I think, were a step in the right direction, but certainly not sufficient to cover the tremendous cost involved in providing sufficient and adequate protection at these railway crossings. In 1958 another amendment to the Railway Act was passed, and the amount of money that could be spent on this type of work was increased. As a matter of fact, $10 million additional for a period of three years was also provided. Also at this time the contributions to be made from this fund for level crossings was raised from 60 per cent to 80 per cent, and the work on grade separations was increased from 30 per cent to 50 per cent. There was also an interesting section in the legislation which provided that the fund would contribute to the marking of railway cars.
I feel that this particular legislation is good, but should be studied perhaps a little more closely. I think it is quite economic, but I have not seen too much of it in use. Last autumn I was travelling along the highway, of course within the speed limit, and the first thing I knew was that I came face to face with a freight car which was rattling across the highway. I did not see any markings, either on any of the cars or on any of the signs, which should have been made in reflective paint. I am not so sure whether it would not be a profitable suggestion that engines, passenger cars, and freight cars should be painted with some phosphorescent or reflective paint over a large portion of them so that they may be seen at night by a driver going along the highway. This is certainly not a solution to the whole problem, but I think there is a definite danger of running into freight cars which are crossing highways when there is not sufficient means of warning in the form of protective signals, and so on.
Has the minister pointed out that the purpose of this resolution is to extend for another period of three years the legislation which was passed in 1958, the additional period to commence after January 31, 1961. We in the opposition, of course, not only do not oppose this legislation but welcome it. However, we cannot help but feel that the government

Railway Act
might just as well have made this legislation permanent instead of legislating for another period of three years because, as a matter of fact, this is one of those steps forward from which there is very little likelihood of returning.
The reason for this, of course, is that the provinces, municipalities and even the public utilities companies have in the past claimed that the payment of their share of the construction of adequate protection against railway crossings imposed too heavy a burden on their finances and, as a matter of fact, did not apply for aid in providing adequate protection at such crossings even though it was definitely required.
I believe this is particularly true with respect to the municipalities. Because of their serious financial handicaps and vast financial obligations and responsibilities, the municipalities have not been able to pay their share of the cost of providing adequate safety measures and I am sure that the extension for a three-year period of the amendments of 1958 will not put them in a position in which they will be able to provide what is in my opinion this absolutely necessary protection.
If I may say so, the weaknesses of this legislation as well as of legislation such as that governing the winter employment program lie in the fact that it is beyond the reach of the municipalities to utilize the benefits attached thereto. I believe that many municipalities cannot afford to pay their share of the cost of this protection whether that share be 5 per cent, 10 per cent or 15 per cent. Unless some solution is found to the problem of the financial responsibilities of municipalities I believe the government should consider this legislation as a permanent thing. Indeed, unless the financial problems of municipalities can be solved the only changes that can possible be foreseen will be continually increasing amounts until all the municipalities would be in a position to provide for their citizens adequate protection against these very tragic accidents.
We on this side of the chamber do not oppose this legislation, as I said, nor do we oppose the extension of the 1958 provisions. I personally cannot help but feel that special consideration or perhaps some special concession should be made to the municipalities which are, I believe, a special case, in order that they may be in a position to take advantage of the legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I, too, would like to extend our welcome to you at seeing you in the position in which we have seen you on many occasions in the past. I am sure we will get along as well in the future as we did in the months gone by.

There has been a fairly thorough coverage of the history of the railway grades crossing fund both by the minister and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres including statistics of the increased number of automobiles and accidents and so on, and I do not think it is necessary for us to dwell on this point at too great length.
I believe that all hon. members in this house and many people throughout Canada are vitally concerned with the safety and well-being of the citizens of this nation. One way in which parliament can contribute toward the safety of Canadian citizens is through assistance in this form and by providing safety facilities at railway grade crossings in terms of underpasses, overpasses, signals and other things.
We welcome the indication by the minister that he wants to extend for an additional three years the amendments that were made in 1958. Without being critical of the intention of the minister and the government I think we must conclude that this represents a haphazard and piecemeal means of accomplishing this end. Because it affects so directly the welfare and safety of our population we should not handle the matter on a day-to-day basis with extensions for periods of two or three years. It would be more in keeping with our desire to provide safe railway crossings and more in keeping with progressive governmental planning if this arrangement were to be made a permanent part of the Canadian statutes.
Unless the minister is working toward the idea of having the federal authorities assume full responsibility for the safety of railway grade crossings there is little advantage in providing these extensions. If the minister is working in this direction this extension will give him some breathing space to work out the details of the assumption by the federal authorities of the entire financial responsibility with respect to these crossings but if that is not the case I must comment that we are operating in a haphazard way in extending existing provisions with no thought of permanency.
The municipalities have a partial financial responsibility in this field where the use of such funds is made within the municipalities. Over the years the municipalities have been forced to accept an increasing financial burden and have witnessed a narrowing of the tax base from which to finance that burden. We could be much more generous to the municipalities. Many of them are in financial difficulties because of the financial policies of a colleague of the Minister of Transport, namely the Minister of Finance. We could alleviate the financial burden of the municipalities by eliminating the need for their

participating financially in the cost of the construction of safety devices at these crossings.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres mentioned a point which I believe needs repeating. When the amendments were introduced in 1958 there was a lengthy discussion about the need for striping, painting or otherwise marking the sides of box cars with some type of phosphorus or luminous paint so they would be noticeable in the evening.
In looking through the debate of the minister's estimates last session I noticed that he told us that orders had already been issued to the railways to proceed with the painting or striping with some sort of phosphorous or luminous paint of the sides of their box cars. He indicated at that time it was too early to say how successful it had been, or whether the railways would co-operate with the desire expressed by the minister and by parliament. Before this resolution passes, I think the minister should indicate to the committee how successful has been the desire expressed by parliament that such luminous paint should be placed on the sides of box cars. He should tell us how they are proceeding and whether his and parliament's desires have been acceptable to the railway companies.
There is another problem which is a sort of extraterritorial one. From time to time we have in Canada quite a number of box cars which are not owned by Canadian railway companies. At times these box cars come from the United States. If Canadian railway companies are going to be required, in the interest of safety, to paint the sides of their box cars with luminous paint, then surely box cars which belong to United States companies should come under the same provision. The minister should give us some indication what the results of any discussions have been, whether those discussions have been carried on by his department or by the Department of External Affairs. How successful have we been in trying to get United States railway companies to paint the sides of their box cars with luminous paint so that they would be in the same condition as box cars of the Canadian railway companies? Perhaps these remarks are sufficient at this stage of the discussion of the resolution. I hope the minister at this stage of the discussion will undertake to deal with and answer some of the questions that we have raised and some of the questions that may be raised in the debate by other participants.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, needless to say I reiterate the remarks that have been made with respect to our pleasure at seeing you back once again to take up your duties. We
Railway Act
appreciate very much the fact that you have been able to return to your duties.
This is an old subject which has been before the house on many occasions. I have spoken on it quite often in the past because it was brought to my attention by the Scarborough section of Danforth riding where they have the very serious problem of a large number of grade level crossings. In the riding there are some 82. I have put these details on the record before. Of these 82, 52 are not in the really serious class at present. Eleven of them require grade separations and the others call for signals and short-arm gates. Toronto also has 38. I will probably cover them later. I may say that when this question was before us various ideas were submitted and some statistics were gone into. The big problem with respect to grade level crossings is the matter of getting the finances to relieve the situation.
When this matter first came before the house the hon. member for Laurier was minister of transport. Later on the then member for St. Antoine-St. George was minister of transport. During the time the hon. member for Laurier was minister of transport a report of a committee was brought in, and it was a very comprehensive one. It went into the matter very thoroughly and set out a good deal of information which was vital. It also covered the history of the grade level crossing fund from its inception in 1909. If my memory serves me aright, the problem from the start was finances. This problem kept the board pretty well occupied. In fact, it taxed their ingenuity because of the inability of the railways and municipalities to meet their share of the cost, as has been brought out by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. In fact, as the program was presented it was almost beyond the capacity of the municipalities and the railways to meet their share of the costs.
The reason the matter was brought before us was that there was a continual demand for action because the accident rate at grade level crossings was growing. Originally the sum of $500,000 was allotted to the grade level crossing fund to improve the situation. I might point out that when the fund started the mode of transportation was quite different from what it is now. It was mostly horse and buggy. Accidents were not happening at a very high rate in those days. The board moved in a lackadaisical manner. If an accident happened in a certain place they would do something about correcting it. The demand was not as pressing as it is now.
Not until the advent of the automobile did conditions at grade level crossings start to become serious. It is doubtful whether they

Railway Act
took the matter seriously into consideration because the amount that was set up to take care of the situation was $500,000. At the present time it is up to $500 million. The commission which was set up increased the amount as the situation warranted. The figure started to mount and the accident rate became more serious. The problems in the urban centres became very demanding. It was taken out of the realm of $1 million.
The report that was brought in covered the situation very thoroughly. It indicated that at that time there were somewhere around
32,000	grade level crossings in the country. To relieve the problem confronting the country the report suggested that it would take at least $5 million. At the time the opposition said that that would not begin to touch the problem before us; that $5 million would not begin to cope with the situation; that $15 million was the least amount that should be considered. Most of the arguments were along that line; nevertheless, the government passed its legislation and raised the amount that could be in the fund to $7 million. The provincial governments were invited to participate and make contributions to the fund and they were told that any condition stipulated would be observed by the transport board. They declined to accept the offer but when the responsibility of the provincial government with respect to highways was pointed out to them they did provide grants to municipalities to help with respect to grade separation.
The situation having been recognized over the years, the federal government increased the amount of its contributions. They started off by contributing 20 per cent of the cost of the project. Then the amount was raised to 40 per cent, then to 60 per cent and at the present time it is 80 per cent. By so doing the share paid by municipalities has decreased proportionately. It used to be 60 per cent, then 30 per cent, then 25 per cent and now it is 12J per cent.
As the railways were the ones that were feeling the pinch most they seldom asked for a level crossing separation to be put in because of the cost involved. They always ducked the situation. However, over the years their share has gone down from 40 per cent to 30 per cent to 15 per cent and now it is down to 7J per cent. As the minister has pointed out, the maximum contribution from the fund for any one level crossing is now $500,000 whereas at the start it used to be $5,000. Grade separations cost a considerable amount of money and therefore it was first provided that no one municipality would be able to have more than three projects in any one year. That was subsequently increased to six projects. But then costs

mounted and the result was that municipalities could not undertake any more than one project at a time unless they had further assistance and that is where the province of Ontario came in when highways crossed railroads and assisted the municipalities, particularly in the Scarborough region.
I have shown the progress that has been made by the board increasing the amount of their contribution in order to help municipalities and the railways. However, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, the fact still remains that in spite of the increased contributions by the federal government the financial burden on the municipalities and the railways is one that they are not able to meet and therefore the problem is coming back to the federal government. It has been suggested by the hon. member for Skeena that probably the federal government should eventually assume the whole burden. I do not know whether it would be advisable to do that or whether there should not be another approach to the problem which is a lot more serious than we think.
I cannot agree with the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres who says that progress has been made and that accidents have decreased because that is not the fact. I think his figures are not correct. There are 75 more level crossings each year on account of the explosive expansion that has taken place in practically all urban centres in Canada. Consequently there are more accidents taking place and the figure is higher. There are approximately 33,212 grade level crossings at the present time and of that number 2,383 are protected by signals and watchmen. There are 1,762 crossings protected by grade separations. There have been many improvements but that is the situation today.
The average cost of protection for a grade crossing is $7,000 and the annual cost of maintenance is $600. Automatic short arm gates and signals cost about $15,000 with annual maintenance amounting to $900. If a municipality has a fair number of such crossings they are faced with the problem of meeting the maintenance cost. It places a very heavy burden upon the municipalities and also upon the railways. They not only have to meet their share of the initial cost but they have to meet the continuing maintenance cost when these installations are made and they are not in a financial position to carry this load.
At the time of the commission report the number of requests that had been submitted for grade level crossing protection was summarized and then the cost was set out. It was pointed out that the average urban project

involving grade level separation cost about $800,000 and the average rural project $100,000. However, in the case of urban projects the cost generally went far beyond this $800,000, in some cases as high as $2,400,000 through exproprations and property damage costs, but the government's share was only $500,000. The provinces had to take a hand and assist the municipalities in order to complete these ventures. It was a very serious problem when the city had to carry the added cost.
I know that Toronto has some 38 grade level crossings that require grade separation. I would say that in the last two years five or six have been taken care of. The city of London has 11, Edmonton has 5 and Hamilton 8. I do not have any figures for Vancouver, Victoria and larger centres like Calgary, Winnipeg and Montreal. However, it was set out by provinces exactly what was required and it involves a terrific amount of money.
I would not say that I was amazed but I was a bit surprised at the remarks of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres about the necessity for grade level crossing protection. I know that the people of Danforth riding and the metro-Toronto officials have requested me to help them in the matter of level crossings. The minister himself has quite a number in his riding that require separation. The hon. member for Greenwood was fortunate enough to have the level crossing at Woodbine avenue and Greenwood taken care of. However, this came about through necessity and not because of any pressure he brought to bear. It was on the program for Toronto and was urgent.
I pointed out that these grade separation projects have an average cost of $800,000 and that at times they cost more. I was surprised that the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres did not press the question. As long as I have been a member of the house no member on the government on the opposition side has ever stated the requirements of the province of Quebec. I know that there are far more grade separations required in Montreal than anywhere else. The city of Quebec had a railway relocation project involving a good many crossings and I can visualize that the number in the province of Quebec must be very great. I thought that the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres would have been able to inform us just how serious the problem is in the province of Quebec. I should like to have the benefit of the figures myself. I know that a lot of these grade level crossings were taken care of when they were building the St. Lawrence seaway project, it being part of its development.
Railway Act
I know that in the province of Quebec they certainly have a lot of grade level crossings. I am bringing this up to show you how serious the problem is. In New Brunswick they set out how many would be required for their major projects and likewise in Nova Scotia. They lumped them together for the Atlantic provinces and this emphasized the magnitude of the problem.
I tell you this because the commissioners reported they set up a hypothetical program that would cost over $700 million over a period of 20 years or $35 million a year. This program would eliminate about 5 per cent of the crossings which they admitted would just scratch the surface. In order to effect a remedial program that could make real progress, an appropriation of $700 million would be required, and probably at today's prices it would be $750 million. This is a program that the municipalities and railways, even at the low percentage of 12J per cent and 7J per cent as a cost-sharing basis, could not support.
The commission set out just how serious this problem was. The hypothetical program, as I have stated, was to be spread over a period of 20 years. As I have pointed out also, if we are going to even attempt to make any real progress an appropriation of $750 million would be required. When you are talking about that amount of money, you must realize that it would account for about one sixth of the total expense budget of the country just to take care of this problem.
Last year, according to the records and contrary to the statement made by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, the accident toll has increased. I believe the hon. member said the accident rate had been decreasing. There were 516 accidents at railway crossings, and 188 people were killed and 662 were injured.

speechtext: I think, at the same time as I gave those figures I also mentioned that the number of motor vehicle registrations had more than doubled.

speechtext:
I will come to that; that is another matter but it is relevant to this problem and, in answer to the hon. member for Skeena, is probably the reason for the policy being established by the government. They are making provision for a sum of $15 million a year for a 3-year period to take care of this problem. As I have mentioned before, even the tremendous sum of $750 million would be insufficient to take care of the real problem, so if we are to take care of the problem there has to be a different approach, that is if we are to eliminate these 516 accidents at level crossings in which 188 were killed and 662 injured.

Railway Act
The board of transport commissioners has worked out what they have called an accident frequency rate per 100 level crossings. This is very interesting data, but I do not believe people are interested in percentage figures of how the death toll is going down. They are interested in stopping accidents. I want to say that the board of transport commissioners has done a wonderful job in connection with this program. They are dedicated to reducing the number of accidents but the number is increasing although the percentage is less, because of the increase in cars using the highways. However, the problem is still serious and the government is to be commended for their approach to it.
As the Minister of Transport has pointed out, in the last 48 years, since the inception of the transport commissioners, only $19 million was spent in attacking this problem. In the two years this government has been in office they have appropriated $15 million a year. We said at the time the program was initiated this was not enough, but it would be a lot better than before. It turns out to be about 200 per cent better than before because there was only $5 million appropriated previously. This government is to be commended because $28 million has been spent in the two previous years, and before the fiscal year is over that sum will probably reach $30 million. In two years they have spent nearly twice as much as previous governments spent in 48 years. We cannot very well condemn them for that when they made a real effort to make work and provide projects urgently needed.
I recall when this matter was under discussion during the previous administration's term of office, and at that time mention was made of the fact that accidents occurred at protected level crossings. I do not refer to those at which there is grade separation, but level crossings where there are short arm gates, wigwags and other signal devices. I do not know whether or not I have the figures here, but in 1958 there were 2,383 accidents at protected crossings, and about 30 per cent of those accidents occurred at night. These accidents happened notwithstanding the protection at the crossings.
In addition to this I should like to mention the terrible toll taken by highway accidents. This is a matter that seemed to be ignored until two or three years ago when the national safety council was formed. We considered that the figures for accidents at grade level crossings were appalling, but 
when we got the figures indicating the number of accidents that happened on the highways of Canada, they were even more appalling. There were 56,733 accidents on the highways, 2,930 people were killed, as compared to 188 at grade level crossings, and 79,399 people were injured on the highway as compared with -662 at grade crossings. While we were astounded by the figures for grade crossing accidents and were criticizing the board of transport commissioners because they would not take a serious view of the problem, we find the problem of highway accidents is even more serious. The national safety council was headed by a former minister of defence, Mr. Brooke Clax-ton, and latterly by the president of the Shell Oil Company, Mr. Ash.
This safety council, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Skeena, requested the railways to standardize signals and signs because the signs were hodgepodge all over the country. They worked on that, and then they came up with a request for fluorescent markings on the box cars so they could be seen at night. These markings were ordered by the board of transport commissioners, but the railways seem to be a law unto themselves. If it suits them they will go along with you, but if they decide it is going to cost money, they ignore orders. Eventually, this will be one of the things we will find necessary to give added protection and prevent people from running into the sides of box cars at night. As I have said, it is startling to find that there were 56,733 highway accidents as compared with 516 accidents at railway crossings. The cost of complete protection is tremendous. The government itself will have to reallocate the cost but not necessarily on the federal government. Every province should be greatly concerned about this highway toll. It is a problem for them as well as for the federal government.
I note that I have just about exhausted my time, Mr. Chairman, but before sitting down I should like again to commend the government and the Minister of Transport on having given us a progressive policy. I hope they will get around to the program which was set out by the board of transport commissioners in that hypothetical scheme they had with respect to spreading a large sum of money- I will say $750 million-spread over Canada will reduce the death toll considerably. This mounting death toll cannot be countenanced for long by sane people who have any respect for the value of life and the welfare of the country. I say that this policy should be

applied generally all over the country, with no particular place being favoured above another. We will see how far $15 million will go under circumstances under which $700 million a year would be required in order to attack the problem and to make any progress at all.

Mr. Chairman, while
we are discussing this resolution to extend level crossing grants for another three years after January 31, 1981, I want to avail myself of this opportunity to deal with a matter which the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Eudes), and myself have frequently brought up in the last few years. Indeed, we never failed to deal with the matter on any occasion. I am thinking of the removal of old railway tracks that run across the eastern sector of Montreal, starting at Moreau street, crossing the ridings of Hochelaga, Maisonneuve-Rosemont and Mer-cier, and end up in the extreme north eastern section of the city.
If I am right, those rail tracks are about 50 years old, and, though they have been very useful in their time for the transport of passengers and freight, the position has changed long ago for, today, they are not used for passenger transport any more but only for some freight and tank cars hauling oil from the easternmost limits of Montreal.
That part of the city, once far from the downtown area, is today very densely populated. In addition, many very flourishing business firms, which are in no way behind those in the western part of the city, are located in that eastern area.
Those old tracks are now quite useless as they are not used for passenger transport and only give service to a score of industries in the east. Therefore, if we compare the little use they have today with the numerous inconveniences they cause the people of Montreal, I think that we should avail ourselves of this resolution and attempt to discover means of freeing the people who live in the extreme east of Montreal from such monstrosity which, as I say, is a source of irritation and an obstacle to progress in that sector.
Now, how can we, under our present legislation, hope to get rid of this antiquated trackage? C.N.R. officials have always refused to grant our wishes whenever we have asked them to stop using that line in
Railway Act
favour of another running along Montreal harbour.
The problem, in my opinion, may be considered from two angles. I said a moment ago that it is no longer a passenger line, while it serves only about twenty industries, apart from tank cars. It would be very easy for the Canadian National Railways to use their line along Montreal harbour, which would permit the removal of that old line and the clearance of the whole eastern part of Montreal.
Now, we must face the possibility that Canadian National Railways will obstinately refuse those improvements which have been asked for so many years. Now, if they refuse to go ahead on their own with the removal of that railway track, there is, it seems, a way of achieving our purpose, under the amendment of 1955, and of 1958, or else in basing our claims on this legislation. In fact, several associations, such as the businessmen's association of the eastern part of Montreal, for instance, could exert pressure-in resorting to the railway act- upon the city of Montreal, in order that an inquiry be made by the transport commission, because I believe that if such an inquiry were made, a favourable report would be submitted to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), and there would then be a possibility of solution, on the basis of this bill.
It is therefore simply a case of doing justice to the people of eastern Montreal.
As the hon. member who spoke before me has pointed out, there are enormous problems, and important improvements have to be made all over this country; but I do not believe we can find anywhere else in Canada another place where railway tracks cut across urban centres, as is the case at present in the constituencies of Maisonneuve-Rosemont, Hochelaga and Mercier.

I said I would appreciate if he would take note of those questions so that I could expect an answer within the next two weeks. I should

like to know whether there is between the authorities of the C.N.R. and the authorities of the city of Montreal a contract which permits the trains of the C.N.R. actually to cross in the east end of Montreal from the old Moreau station up to the far east end of Montreal. Now, Mr. Chairman, there is also a clash of interests, as we have already pointed out many times to C.N.R. officials.
In the first place there is the human element, in that for so many years people in eastern Montreal have had to put up with the inconvenience of that railway line. On the other hand, there is the financial interest of the Canadian National.
I hope that the human element will be considered before everything else. I trust that the bill which will soon come before the house will enable us to rid eastern Montreal of this useless railway line.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to extend to you a hearty welcome and tell you how happy we are to see that your health has improved.
I shall be brief. I merely want to point out a special problem facing part of my constituency. In fact in my constituency four municipalities, Chateau-Richer, Beau-pre, Ste. Anne de Beaupre and St. Joachim, have to put up with at least eight of those level crossings.
It is known that last year those municipalities were served by a train travelling back and forth between Quebec and St. Joachim; that train used to be called "the little train to St. Joachim".
For financial reasons, that service was discontinued with the result that today only one train-the Quebec-La Malbaie train- runs along the Beaupre coast.
[Mr. Deschatelets.I
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that those grade crossings hamper and even paralyse the economic development of the municipalities I just mentioned. I submit that those grade crossings are now useless and that in the past they proved to be very dangerous at all times for car-drivers.
In three years, three major accidents have happened at those railway crossings on the Beaupre coast, and six people were killed.
Geographically, the Beaupre coast is bound on the north by the railroad running along the municipalities of the Beaupre coast. Then, farther north there is the St. Lawrence river and, between the municipalities and the river there is the national highway leading from Quebec to the northern part of the province.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is my impression that the Minister of Transport, in co-operation with the C.N.R. could render great service to those municipalities if grade crossings were eliminated in the following way. I would ask the Minister of Transport to consider this problem.
In my view, there is ample space along the St. Lawrence river, to the south of those municipalities, to build a railway which would in no way impede their economic development. As a service to the people of Beaupre coast, and the municipalities of Chateau-Richer, Ste. Anne de Beaupre and St. Joachim, the C.N.R. might make a survey to find out the cost of building a new railway along the St. Lawrence, including the cost of necessary expropriations. In this way, I am sure the Department of Transport and the C.N.R. would render a tremendous service to the people and would contribute to the economic development of the municipalities involved, which at present are being strangled by a railway which has become completely useless, except to allow trains to go by without even making a stop.
I therefore ask the Minister of Transport to kindly submit my request to the proper authorities of the C.N.R., so that this stretch of railway may be removed as soon as possible, thus enabling the people involved to enjoy the benefits of economic development.
